info.name: relay — API
info.description:
# relay

Every HTTP endpoint the server actually serves, as of this collection being written.

## What is not here, and why

**There are no room, chat or message endpoints yet.** Rooms, conversations, messages, panels and their authorisation exist as schema and as server-side modules (`src/rooms.ts`, `src/access.ts`, `src/actors.ts`) with 58 tests behind them, but nothing routes to them: reads arrive over Electric shapes (Phase 2, the shape proxy) and writes over a write endpoint (Phase 3). Neither is built. Nothing was invented here to fill the gap.

## Getting a session

AuthKit owns the sign-in round trip, so a session cannot be minted from Postman.

1. `pnpm run up && pnpm dev`
2. Sign in at <http://localhost:5173>
3. Copy the `relay_session` cookie value (DevTools → Application → Cookies)
4. Paste it into the collection's **session** variable

The server accepts the same sealed value as `Authorization: Bearer`, so the browser cookie and the Postman bearer are interchangeable. Folder 1 also has the desktop PKCE path, which mints its own verifier.

## Token refresh

A seal expires. When the server refreshes one mid-request it returns the new seal in the body as `refreshedSession` for bearer callers, and a collection-level script rolls `{{session}}` forward automatically — so a long Postman run does not fall over.

exec: // A refreshed access token comes back in the body for bearer callers.
// Roll {{session}} forward so the collection keeps working across a token expiry.
} catch (e) { /* not JSON — redirects and 204s land here */ }

variable.description: The relay_session cookie value; sent as a bearer token

item.name: 1 · Signing in
item.description:
AuthKit owns the round trip, so a session cannot be minted from Postman. Two of these are browser-only and are here to be read, not sent.

**The practical path:** run `pnpm dev`, sign in at http://localhost:5173, then copy the `relay_session` cookie value into the collection's `session` variable. The server accepts the same sealed value as `Authorization: Bearer`, so everything else here then works.

item.name: Login (browser) — open in a browser, not here

request.description:
303 to AuthKit. Sets `relay_oauth`, a short-lived cookie holding the state this browser must send back — `/auth/callback` refuses anything else, which is what stops a login CSRF.

Postman will follow the redirect to WorkOS and you will get their sign-in HTML. That is expected; finish the flow in a real browser.

item.name: Login (desktop PKCE) — mints a verifier for the next request

request.description:
The desktop shell holds the PKCE verifier and sends only its S256 challenge, so the code that comes back can be redeemed by nothing else.

The pre-request script generates a fresh verifier/challenge pair into collection variables. Open the resulting URL in a browser, sign in, and the handoff page hands you a `code` — paste it into **Exchange**.

exec: // PKCE S256, the way the desktop shell does it.
for (let i = 0; i < 64; i++) verifier += chars[Math.floor(Math.random() * chars.length)];

request.description:
WorkOS redirects here. Needs the `relay_oauth` cookie set by `/auth/login` in the **same** browser, so sending it from Postman lands on `/sign-in?error=state_mismatch` by design.

Browser surface: exchanges the code and sets `relay_session`.
Desktop surface: returns the handoff HTML instead, because only the shell holds the verifier.

Redeems the code, proving possession of the verifier whose challenge went out with the authorize request. Returns `{ sealedSession, user }`.

On success the test script writes `sealedSession` into `{{session}}` — after this, every other request in the collection is authenticated.

item.name: 2 · Session and tenancy
item.description: Everything here needs `{{session}}`. A 401 is a normal answer, not a failure — it is what every authorisation decision downstream keys off.

request.description:
The session is `{user_id, organization_id}` and nothing else — **workspace is never in it** (invariant 3). Slack put it there, it became their shard key, and they spent years unwinding it.

Roles come from our Postgres mirror rather than the seal, so a role change shows up immediately instead of on the next token refresh.

exec: // A refreshed access token comes back in the body for bearer callers.
// Roll {{session}} forward so the collection keeps working across a token expiry.
} catch (e) { /* not JSON — redirects and 204s land here */ }

item.name: Sign up — create an org and its default workspace

request.description:
The single signup path — solo, startup and enterprise alike:

`org → org membership (owner) → default workspace → workspace membership (admin) → actor`

The actor is written inside the same advisory-locked transaction, because an account without one is real and cannot be added to any room.

Serialised per user with a Postgres advisory lock: creating a WorkOS organization is **not** idempotent — verified against the live API, where two requests with the same `Idempotency-Key` produced two organizations — and nothing in the product can merge duplicates. Call it twice; the second finds the first and reuses it.

Re-issues the session into the new org, so the response carries a fresh seal.

exec: pm.test('status is 200 or 202 or 400 or 401 or 502', () => pm.expect(pm.response.code).to.be.oneOf([200, 202, 400, 401, 502]));
// A refreshed access token comes back in the body for bearer callers.
// Roll {{session}} forward so the collection keeps working across a token expiry.
} catch (e) { /* not JSON — redirects and 204s land here */ }

request.description:
One row per **workspace membership**, not per organization: being in the org is not being in the workspace (invariant 5). Each row carries its organization so the client knows whether opening it is a navigation or a session re-issue.

Captures the first `organizationId` into `{{organizationId}}` for the switch below.

exec: // A refreshed access token comes back in the body for bearer callers.
// Roll {{session}} forward so the collection keeps working across a token expiry.
} catch (e) { /* not JSON — redirects and 204s land here */ }

request.description:
In the organization the session already names. No WorkOS call and no re-issued session — a workspace is ours, nothing upstream knows about it, and workspace is navigation state rather than a claim.

The creator joins as `admin` and is the only member: a workspace is not visible to the rest of the org by being created. 403 unless you may invite.

exec: // A refreshed access token comes back in the body for bearer callers.
// Roll {{session}} forward so the collection keeps working across a token expiry.
} catch (e) { /* not JSON — redirects and 204s land here */ }

request.description:
Re-issues the session rather than editing a claim, because the target org's authentication requirements may differ — an org enforcing SSO will reject a session established by password, and the only way in is a fresh IdP round trip.

Membership is checked against our mirror, not WorkOS: same data, already local, and this must not become a network round trip on a menu click.

exec: // A refreshed access token comes back in the body for bearer callers.
// Roll {{session}} forward so the collection keeps working across a token expiry.
} catch (e) { /* not JSON — redirects and 204s land here */ }

request.description:
With `Authorization` set: revokes the session upstream and returns 204. The caller holds the seal, so there is no cookie to clear.

Without it: 303 to WorkOS's logout URL, clearing `relay_session`.

Clears `{{session}}` afterwards, so run it last.

item.name: 3 · Invitations
item.description: WorkOS owns invitations — they are a first-class resource there, and acceptance happens in their UI, so there is no request of ours to hook. It surfaces later as an `organization_membership.created` webhook.

request.description: Pending invitations for the organization the session names. 400 if it names none.

`role` is one of `admin`, `member`, `guest`. 403 unless you may invite.

**A guest is not a lesser member** — they get an org membership and *no* workspace membership, and see only the rooms they are explicitly added to. That is why guests never needed FGA: the check stays a primary-key lookup.

Note the invitation creates a `pending` membership. No workspace access and no actor exist until it flips to `active` — a revoked invitation that had already granted a workspace row was a real bug, found exactly that way.

exec: pm.test('status is 201 or 400 or 401 or 403 or 502', () => pm.expect(pm.response.code).to.be.oneOf([201, 400, 401, 403, 502]));

request.description: 204 on success. 403 unless you may invite.

item.name: 4 · Webhooks
item.description:
WorkOS is upstream and Postgres is a read replica (invariant 4). These rows are written by this handler and by signup, and nowhere else.

**Locally this is unreachable from WorkOS** without a tunnel — `pnpm tunnel` sets one up and re-points WorkOS in one step. The request below is here to show the shape and to prove the signature check rejects an unsigned body.

request.description:
401, and deliberately without saying why — a verification oracle is a gift to whoever is probing.

Fields arrive **camelCase** (`firstName`, not `first_name`) because `constructEvent` deserialises them. An earlier version read snake_case and silently mirrored every name as null; the tests passed because they asserted the same wrong shape.

Handled: `user.created/updated/deleted`, `organization.created/updated/deleted`, `organization_membership.created/updated/deleted`. Anything else gets a 200 — anything other than 200 makes WorkOS retry forever.

`user.updated` also carries the rename out to `actors.display_name`, which is a projection of this mirror maintained by this handler alone.

exec: pm.test('an unsigned body is refused', () => pm.response.to.have.status(401));
